# A Brief History of Lighthouses

For as long as people have sailed, they have needed a way to find land safely in the dark. The earliest navigational lights were simply fires kindled on hilltops, later raised on platforms to extend their reach. From these beginnings grew one of humanity's most enduring structures.

The most famous ancient lighthouse was the Pharos of Alexandria, completed around 280 BCE under Ptolemy II. Rising more than 100 metres, it was among the tallest structures of the ancient world and one of its Seven Wonders. A fire at its summit, possibly reflected by polished metal, guided ships into Egypt's busy harbour for well over a thousand years before earthquakes brought it down. Its name survives in the word for lighthouse in several languages, including the French *phare* and Spanish *faro*. The Romans carried the idea across their empire, building towers at Ostia, Dover, and La Coruña, where the Tower of Hercules still operates today.

After Rome's decline, lighthouse building waned. Medieval lights were often maintained by monks or local communities, burning wood, coal, or candles in modest towers. The revival came with expanding maritime trade. France's Cordouan lighthouse, finished in 1611, combined engineering with palatial grandeur.

The eighteenth century brought the challenge of building on wave-swept rocks. The Eddystone reef off Plymouth saw four successive towers. The first, Henry Winstanley's, was swept away in the Great Storm of 1703 with its builder inside. John Smeaton's 1759 design proved decisive: he used interlocking granite blocks, hydraulic lime that set underwater, and a curved profile modelled on an oak tree. His tower became the template for rock lighthouses worldwide, and Robert Stevenson's Bell Rock lighthouse of 1810 refined it further.

Illumination improved alongside masonry. Aimé Argand's hollow-wick oil lamp of the 1780s gave a steady, bright flame, and parabolic reflectors concentrated it. The great breakthrough came in 1822, when Augustin-Jean Fresnel devised a lens of concentric prisms that gathered light into a powerful beam visible for more than twenty miles. Fresnel lenses soon crowned towers on every coast, and distinctive flash patterns let mariners identify each light.

Fuel shifted from whale oil to kerosene, then gas, and finally electricity. In the twentieth century, automation steadily ended the solitary profession of the lighthouse keeper; most lights were unmanned by the 1990s.

Today satellite navigation has reduced the lighthouse's practical importance, yet many still shine as backups and landmarks. Preserved as museums and monuments, they remain powerful symbols of vigilance, guidance, and safety.
